What's new in Battlefield 1.3

Source: vignettes/articles/new-in-1-3.Rmd
new-in-1-3.Rmd

This article walks through the functions added or changed in Battlefield 1.3 (Bioconductor devel). All examples use the simulated data shipped with the package, so they can be run as they are.

  • Splitting a scattered cluster: split_clusters(), add_split_to_spe(), clean_orphans()
  • Layers where core and border never touch: create_cluster_layers() with center and core_radius
  • Picking spots interactively: view_spots()
  • Neighbourhood of a spot given by its coordinates: get_neighborhood_spots()
  • Gene trends along a trajectory: compare_gene_trends() 
library(Battlefield)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(ggplot2)

We use the simulated Visium HD 16 µm slide, and keep its coordinates and cluster labels in a data frame, as in the main vignette.

data("visiumHD_16um_simulated_spe", package = "Battlefield")
spe <- visiumHD_16um_simulated_spe
df <- data.frame(
  spot_id = colnames(spe),
  x = spatialCoords(spe)[, 1],
  y = spatialCoords(spe)[, 2],
  cluster = as.character(spe$cluster)
)

A small helper draws spots coloured by any column:

plot_spots <- function(d, col, palette = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, fill = .data[[col]])) +
    geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.6, colour = "grey60", stroke = 0.2) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = col) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
  if (!is.null(palette)) p <- p + scale_fill_manual(values = palette,
                                                    na.value = "grey90")
  p
}
plot_spots(df, "cluster")

Splitting a scattered cluster

A clustering method can give the same label to regions that are far apart. Layers, borders or trajectories computed on such a cluster then mix several regions. To mimic this, we merge clusters 2 and 5, which do not touch, into a single cluster X, and add three isolated X spots inside cluster 4.

df_x <- df
df_x$cluster[df_x$cluster %in% c("2", "5")] <- "X"
orphans <- c(closest_spot(df_x, 12000, 7600)$spot_id,
             closest_spot(df_x, 1200, 8800)$spot_id,
             closest_spot(df_x, 8000, 1600)$spot_id)
df_x$cluster[df_x$spot_id %in% orphans] <- "X"
table(df_x$cluster)
#> 
#>   1   3   4   X 
#>  81 427 409  83

split_clusters() finds the contiguous pieces of one cluster. Pieces of at least min_size spots are renamed X_1, X_2, … from largest to smallest; smaller pieces (the orphans) keep the label X.

split <- split_clusters(df_x, "X", min_size = 5)
table(split$cluster_split)
#> 
#>   1   3   4   X X_1 X_2 
#>  81 427 409   3  47  33
plot_spots(split, "cluster_split")

To split several clusters, call it again with cluster_col = "cluster_split". add_split_to_spe() stores the labels in the colData, matched by spot_id, without changing the original cluster column:

spe_x <- spe
spe_x$cluster <- df_x$cluster
spe_x <- add_split_to_spe(spe_x, split)
table(spe_x$cluster, spe_x$cluster_split)
#>    
#>       1   3   4   X X_1 X_2
#>   1  81   0   0   0   0   0
#>   3   0 427   0   0   0   0
#>   4   0   0 409   0   0   0
#>   X   0   0   0   3  47  33

clean_orphans() removes the pieces of a cluster smaller than min_size. Spots of other clusters are always kept.

cleaned <- clean_orphans(df_x, "X", min_size = 5)
setdiff(df_x$spot_id, cleaned$spot_id)
#> [1] "bin16_884" "bin16_181" "bin16_791"

To clean layers, compute them with all spots first, then remove the orphans from the result, so that the orphans still count as neighbours when layers are defined:

layers_x <- create_cluster_layers(df_x, "X", k = 8)
layers_x <- clean_orphans(layers_x, "X", min_size = 5)
table(layers_x$layer)
#> 
#>       border         core intermediate 
#>           55            2           23

Layers where core and border never touch

create_cluster_layers() classifies the spots of a cluster into border, intermediate and core. Since 1.3, every spot touching a border spot is intermediate, so core and border are never in contact. A narrow cluster can therefore have no core at all.

layer_cols <- c(border = "#d7301f", intermediate = "#fdbb84",
                core = "#2b8cbe")
layers <- create_cluster_layers(df, target_cluster = "4", k = 8)
table(layers$layer)
#> 
#>       border         core intermediate 
#>           88          151          172
plot_spots(merge(df, layers[, c("spot_id", "layer")], all.x = TRUE),
           "layer", layer_cols)

The new center argument places the core around a chosen spot, given by its identifier or by its coordinates. Border spots are unchanged; core spots are the non-border spots closest to center, either within core_radius (in coordinate units) or, by default, the closest 1 - intermediate_quantile share.

core <- layers[layers$layer == "core", ]
center <- closest_spot(core, 12800, 7200)$spot_id
layers_c <- create_cluster_layers(df, target_cluster = "4", k = 8,
                                  center = center, core_radius = 1500)
table(layers_c$layer)
#> 
#>       border         core intermediate 
#>           88           40          283
plot_spots(merge(df, layers_c[, c("spot_id", "layer")], all.x = TRUE),
           "layer", layer_cols) +
  geom_point(data = df[df$spot_id == center, ], shape = 4, size = 4,
             stroke = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(x, y))

Picking spots interactively

view_spots() draws the spots on an interactive plotly map, over the slide image when the object holds one (the simulated data have none). Hover a spot to see its identifier and coordinates; click spots, or use the box and lasso tools, to select them. A panel then gives the R code to copy: a spots vector and, for one or two spots, data frames A and B ready for build_one_trajectory() or build_similar_trajectories().

Try it below: the map is live.

view_spots(spe, color_by = "cluster")

With a real Visium object, image_file and scale_factor let you use another image than the stored one, and file writes the viewer to a self-contained HTML page that can be shared.

Neighbourhood of a spot given by its coordinates

get_neighborhood_spots() and count_neighborhood() now accept, as spot_id, a one-row data frame with the exact coordinates of a spot, such as A copied from view_spots(). Passing several spots is now an error.

A <- data.frame(x = 4000, y = 4400)   # a spot at the 3 / 4 interface
nb <- get_neighborhood_spots(df, spot_id = A, k = 24)
table(nb$neighborhood)
#> 
#>  3  4 
#> 14 10

Gene trends along a trajectory

compare_gene_trends() tests whether genes decrease or increase along trajectories built with build_similar_trajectories() and stored by add_trajectories_to_spe(). The spots are fixed; only the genes change.

For each gene, the slope (change in expression from the start to the end of the trajectory) comes from a generalized least squares model whose residuals can be spatially correlated, so neighbouring spots are not counted as independent observations. P-values are one-sided, adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg, and r_curve measures how similar each smoothed profile is to that of a reference gene.

We first build parallel trajectories from the centre of cluster 3 to the centre of cluster 4:

centroids <- compute_centroids(df)
A <- centroids[centroids$cluster == 3, c("x", "y")]
B <- centroids[centroids$cluster == 4, c("x", "y")]
trajs <- build_similar_trajectories(df, A, B, top_n = 12, n_extra = 2,
                                    side = "both")
length(unique(trajs$trajectory_id))
#> [1] 5

The simulated slide holds a single gene, so we simulate a reference gene and three genes that decrease, increase or stay flat along the trajectory:

set.seed(1)
pos <- rep(0.5, nrow(df))
pos[match(trajs$spot_id, df$spot_id)] <- trajs$pos_on_seg
sim <- function(slope) 3 + slope * pos + rnorm(length(pos), sd = 0.3)
logcounts <- rbind(REF = sim(-2), DOWN = sim(-1.5), UP = sim(1.5),
                   FLAT = sim(0))
colnames(logcounts) <- df$spot_id
toy <- SpatialExperiment(
  assays = list(logcounts = logcounts),
  spatialCoords = as.matrix(df[, c("x", "y")])
)
toy <- add_trajectories_to_spe(toy, trajectory = trajs)
res <- compare_gene_trends(toy, genes = c("DOWN", "UP", "FLAT"),
                           reference = "REF")
res
#>   gene      slope    r_curve     fdr_down       fdr_up   trend    status
#> 1  REF -1.8237565  1.0000000           NA           NA     ref reference
#> 2 DOWN -1.6949907  0.9960631 3.499210e-13 1.000000e+00     dec    tested
#> 3 FLAT -0.1801978  0.8093483 1.212369e-01 1.000000e+00 unknown    tested
#> 4   UP  1.6096922 -0.9953335 1.000000e+00 1.261951e-15     inc    tested

The smoothed profiles, pooled over all lines, are returned in attr(res, "curves"):

ggplot(attr(res, "curves"), aes(position, mean, colour = gene)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Position on the trajectory (0 = cluster 3, 1 = cluster 4)",
       y = "Smoothed expression", colour = NULL)

A spatial pattern about as long as the trajectory cannot be told apart from a trend, so the FDR stay optimistic in that case: use them to rank genes within a sample, and replicate across samples to conclude. Do not use the gene that guided the choice of trajectory as evidence.
